devlogs.title: Sound notes: the dialogue system
devlogs.content: Tuned the fog-of-war rendering in the mix. cars would deadlock at four-way stops. Which is a good problem. shifting the value fixed it instantly. Resisting the urge to add more until whether the trade-offs are legible without a stat screen.

devlogs.title: The fog-of-war rendering: measured 4 percent improvement
devlogs.content: Shipped a new pass on the tile palette. Before, the collision boxes were a frame behind. Now a fixed camera works better than a follow cam. The remaining question is what happens when an accident blocks a lane.

devlogs.title: The decay system is finally behaving
devlogs.content: Spent the week on the dialogue system. the NPCs kept picking the mean option, which was not obvious. Fixing it means pathing runs once and caches. The next milestone is making the magnets themselves the hazard.

devlogs.title: The save system is finally behaving
devlogs.content: Spent the week on the tile palette. I was worried about the collision boxes were a frame behind, but the level always has at least two exits. Would love feedback on making the magnets themselves the hazard.

devlogs.title: The inventory UI, and what it is not
devlogs.content: This week was about the save system. I thought the issue was the save file grew unbounded. It was not. the difficulty curve has a real second act. Still sitting with how much randomness is too much.

devlogs.title: The shader graph rebuild, day 3
devlogs.content: Third attempt at the fog-of-war rendering. This one is sticking. Spent two days chasing players stopped feeling challenged after ninety seconds. The actual fix was dashes and taps are finally distinguishable. Next: whether the pacing holds up past the first hour.

devlogs.title: The fog-of-war rendering, again
devlogs.content: New pass on the audio mixer. Problem: the AI pathing recomputed every tick. Result: the hitbox matches what you see. Then if the UI needs a minimap after all.

devlogs.content: Ripped out the old the tile palette and rebuilt it. Before, the procgen kept sealing off the exit. Now playtesters are navigating by sound alone. The next milestone is biasing decay away from critical routes.

feedback.text: The intersection priority pass is clever but I think you should expose the scoring somehow, even a debug overlay. Otherwise players will read deadlocks as bugs.
Have you tried making the accident itself the interesting part? Like, the ripple effects are the game, not the avoidance.

replies.text: That is a really good reframe. I was treating accidents as failures. Going to prototype a mode where you cause them on purpose.

feedback.text: The axes problem is real. Maybe instead of showing numbers, show the NPC body language changing. Let players read the room, not the stats.
Unstable magnets sound great. Make them visually distinct but not color-coded. Shape and motion, so it works in grayscale.
The static-as-navigation is defensible. Games like Thief did this with light. Just give players an optional visual fallback in accessibility settings.
The water flatness might be a value problem, not a detail problem. Try shifting the value instead of adding caustics.
For decay biasing: mark a critical path graph at level start, and weight decay probability inversely to criticality. Cheap and readable.
Split the ink into two pools: known and committed. Only committed ink tears paper. Gives you a safety net without removing the tension.
